newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Dixons awaits clarification on tax.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Dixons awaits clarification on tax.

text.p: British electricals retailer Dixons Group Plc said on Wednesday it was still assessing the potential impact of tax proposals in the budget on its extended warranties business.
Dixons shares tumbled on Tuesday in response to tax measures in Chancellor Kenneth Clarke's annual budget which potentially affect insurance polices sold with consumer durables.
But Dixons said the implications of the proposals were not clear. "Having looked at it we don't believe the proposals are aimed at our cover plan policies," said a company spokesman.
But he said until the company had seen the proposals in detail it was difficult to judge any impact.

On Tuesday Clarke proposed an increase in insurance premium tax to 17.5 percent from 2.5 percent on insurance policies sold alongside consumer goods, raising it to the same level as VAT. He also raised insurance premium tax for stand-alone policies to four percent.

Thorn Plc, whose shares also came under pressure, said the tax increase could apply to its television and electricals rentals business, but the company was waiting for clarification from Customs and Excise.
"It may well apply to us," a company spokesman said.
Retail analysts said the key issue was the extent to which the 17.5 percent tax would affect the firms' warranty business and this was still unclear.
They said if it did apply to Dixons it could potentially wipe between five and 10 percent off profits.
"Dixons would probably pass on the tax increase to customers so there would be a volume impact on sales," said one analyst.

Analysts said although the wording of the proposal was not clear, and it looked as though insurers such as Norwich Union, which also sell warranties, would only face an increase in insurance premium tax to four percent.
"For Dixons the worst case scenario would be if they were treated differently from competitors," the analyst said.

Thorn, which rents televisions and other electrical goods, has a rental charge that includes an element of insurance to cover repairs. Currently the insurance payment carries a 2.5 percent insurance premium tax.
The Thorn spokesman said it was too early to say if the company would pass on the increased tax to customers as it was still not clear if it was applicable to Thorn's business.
Thorn's shares were 12 pence lower at 272, while Dixons were 8.5 pence lower at 542 pence.
Worries about the increase in tax also hit Kingfisher Plc because its Comet electricals chain also sells insurance policies with electrical appliances.
A spokesman said the company was still trying to find out whether the tax increase would apply to its policies.
He said if the tax did apply, the impact on Kingfisher would be marginal as Comet only accounts for a small part of the group's overall business.
Kingfisher's shares stood seven pence lower at 617.5.
